title: Graphs and neighbours
summary: Describe places and links with a graph. Read the neighbours of one place from a small table and compare directed and undirected edges.
introduction: Think of three playgrounds joined by paths. The places are points, and the paths connect them. A graph lets a program describe such connections without forcing them into one long line.
learningObjectives: Read one row of an adjacency matrix
Distinguish a direct neighbour from a reachable place

blocks.text: A **graph** holds points called **vertices**, also called nodes. A link between two vertices is an **edge**. A **neighbour** is a vertex joined by one direct edge.
Our vertices are numbered 0, 1, and 2. There is a path between 0 and 1, and a path between 0 and 2. There is no direct path between 1 and 2.
These paths work both ways, so this is an **undirected** graph. A **directed** graph uses arrows: an edge from 0 to 1 does not automatically give an edge from 1 to 0.
An **adjacency matrix** is a square table of connections. Row a, column b is 1 when an edge goes from a to b, and 0 when it does not. Each row and column stands for one vertex.

items: Write row 0 as [0, 1, 1]. Vertex 0 has no edge to itself, but it has edges to 1 and 2.
Write row 1 as [1, 0, 0] and row 2 as [1, 0, 0], because the paths go both ways.
Choose vertex 0. Scan its row from column 0 through column 2.
Print the column number whenever the cell is 1. This prints neighbours 1 and 2.

blocks.text: Choose one tab. All six programs do the same task and print the same result. JavaScript can run here. The other languages need the separate local tools in [Language setup](/tutorials/data-structures-algorithms/language-setup).

blocks.text: The loop visits columns in number order, so the output order is fixed. Vertex 1 can reach vertex 2 by going through 0, but it is not a direct neighbour of 2. Listing neighbours is one step; finding whole routes needs a graph search.
Check the small and tricky cases
An **isolated vertex** has no edges, so its row contains only zeros and prints nothing. A graph may have separate groups that are not connected. A general graph can also contain cycles.
This graph has no self-edges and at most one edge between a pair. A self-edge would appear on the diagonal, such as row 0, column 0. Different problems may allow or forbid these edges.

For V vertices, scanning one matrix row takes O(V) work and the full matrix uses O(V²) space. An **adjacency list** instead stores only each vertex's neighbours. That often saves space when few pairs have edges; the whole list uses O(V + E) space for V vertices and E edges.

items: The output becomes just 0. Vertex 1 is directly joined to 0, but it is not directly joined to 2.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: For an undirected edge, update both directions. If you set row 0, column 1 to 1 but leave row 1, column 0 at 0, the table no longer describes that two-way path.
